catalog_quote: § 5. Stress plays a major role in Hawrami. Its position alone may either distinguish between otherwise identical forms or entail certain morphological consequences. ... (a) Each word has one invariable loud stress, the position of which is not predictable except within certain inflectional patterns. ... Words, or phrases, of three or more syllables may also have an appreciable secondary stress, marked [(-], the position of which bears no fixed relation to that of the main stress. ... In these examples the stress pattern is determined by the fixed order of precedence of the stresses of the various prefixes, stems, endings and suffixes. (b) The only examples of a shift of stress away from the normal pattern occur when a vowel irregularly loses its syllabic character. Its stress is then taken by the following syllable. ... (c) Sentence stress differs only in degree from word stress. ... § …

audit.reasoning: (1) Quote confirmed verbatim in the held archive.org scanned of MacKenzie 1966 at sec. 5 pp. 11-12 and sec. 30 pp. 36-37. (2) The classification rests on a 1966 139-pp grammatical sketch of Luhon Hawrami that remained the standard description until Mohammadirad's 2026 LangSci reference grammar of Tekht Hawrami, which we hold but the record does not cite. I read its sec. 3.3 (pp. 72-78): it calls Hewramî stress 'phonemic', shows stress-only minimal pairs in verbs (beró 'he takes' vs béro 'that he takes', with intensity figures), gives masculine nouns a word-final default and most feminine nouns penultimate stress with a lexical subset of feminines word-final, lists stressed vs unstressed affixes/clitics, and says adjective stress 'is not completely predictable'. sources.quote: p. 72: 'Hewramî is a language with phonemic stress placement: for the majority of verbs, stress is the only cue to distinguish between subjunctive and indicative verbs derived from the present tense ... In Hewramî, there is variability in the positioning of stress in the words. In most cases, this is determined by the lexical category of the words and the interaction between syntax and discourse.' 'Lexical stress is associated with high intensity' (Fig. 3.12). sec. 3.3.1 p. 73: 'Masculine nouns follow what may be considered the general rule of word-final stress placement' (pîyá, sawró, gicî́);

sources.quote: p. 4: 'these varieties have a complicated stress accent system. Verbal stress is characterized by a spike in amplitude and a rising f0. In the case of the stress-attracting prefix ni-, the amplitude spikes on the prefix but the high tone target falls on the following syllable.' p. 6 (Bizłane, Text and Luhon varieties): 'The indicative form is distinguished from the subjunctive only by stress placement on the final syllable, e.g., keró "s/he makes". The subjunctive is formed with stress on the initial syllable, e.g., kéro "(that) s/he makes". These forms are negated with the negative indicative
sources.note: Only recent paper with an explicit (brief, partly acoustic) characterization of Hewramî verbal stress (amplitude spike + rising f0; indicative keró vs subjunctive kéro distinguished by stress alone in Luhon/Text); supports the contrastive/morphological reading. downloaded and read.
